title: BBC radio’s Choral Evensong turned 100; its psalms fit one 7-bar tune to every verse
body: On 7 October 2026 Choral Evensong on BBC radio turned 100: the first broadcast, on 7 October 1926, came live from London’s Westminster Abbey, and it is still heard every week on Radio 3, the BBC’s longest-running outside broadcast, as the MP Jonathan Davies noted [in the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/oct/07/evensong-bbc-centenary-choral-music-jonathan-davies-mp). Its psalms and canticles, such as the Magnificat, are prose whose verses come in every length, and choirs sing them to [Anglican chant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_chant): a short harmonised tune of 7 bars for each verse, or 14 for a pair. The trick is the reciting notes in bars 1 and 4, where all the words of that part are sung on one chord at the pace of careful speech; in a bar of two notes, everything but the last syllable goes on the first. Printed psalters ‘point’ the text, marking each bar line with a sign like an apostrophe and the middle of the verse with a colon. So in the Magnificat the same note carries ‘My soul doth’ in verse 1, seven syllables, ‘For he that is mighty hath’, in verse 4, and just ‘For’ in verse 2.

slides.prompt: One Magnificat verse has 9 words and another 15, yet a choir at evensong sings every verse to the same 7-bar tune. How?
slides.answer: One note stretches: a reciting note holds as many words as needed.
slides.detail: Bars 1 and 4 of an Anglican chant are reciting notes. The words of that part are sung on one chord at speaking pace, then the last few syllables fit the moving notes.

slides.alt: Animation in slate blue and candle gold under a faint Gothic arch: an old radio and a timeline from 1926 to 2026; a 7-bar chant on a staff whose reciting notes in bars 1 and 4 widen to hold the words; a parchment psalter verse with red pointing marks; three Magnificat verses sung to one tune.

slides.prompt: Sing the first four verses of the Magnificat to the same chant. Find the verse whose reciting note has to carry the most syllables.
slides.takeaway: Verse 4: seven syllables, ‘For he that is mighty hath’, on one note; verse 2 has just ‘For’. The tune never changes. The reciting notes stretch, so prose of any length fits.

slides.question: In Anglican chant, what lets one short tune fit psalm verses of very different lengths?
options: Reciting notes that hold many words
The choir skips some of the words
Each verse gets a tune of its own
Long verses are sung faster throughout
slides.explanation: Bars 1 and 4 are reciting notes: all the words of that part go on one chord, sung at speaking pace. In the Magnificat that is one syllable in verse 2 and seven in verse 4.
